newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian Fracmaster CEO to sell stake.
newsitem.headline: Canadian Fracmaster CEO to sell stake.

text.p: Oil services firm Canadian Fracmaster Ltd. said on Wednesday that Chairman Alfred Balm would sell his C$550 million ($396 million) majority stake and resign as chief executive.

The move, which ends years of speculation about the Geneva-based businessman's closely held 67.5 percent interest in Calgary-based Fracmaster, signaled a new era for the once-struggling international company.

"The company is realizing significant growth under its continuing management. I believe it is time for me to retire from my role as chief executive officer," Balm, well-known in Calgary as a local booster and philanthropist, said in a statement released late Tuesday.
Fracmaster said would it would file a preliminary prospectus on Wednesday outlining the proposed secondary offering of common shares through instalment receipts.
The offering, underwritten by Newcrest Capital Inc. and a syndicate of other Canadian brokerages, would be made only in Canada, the company said.
After the transaction is completed in September, President Les Margetak will become chief executive, the company said.
Balm, who took Fracmaster public in 1993, owns 28.9 million shares, which at their current price are worth almost C$550 million ($396 million).

Fracmaster provides high-tech oil well cementing, fracturing and coiled tubing services in the North American energy sector and takes oil in return for well stimulation services in Russian joint ventures. It also performs a growing number of fee-for-service well operations in Russia.
In June, the company expanded its operations by signing a five-year deal with the government of China to rehabilitate 720 oil wells in that country.
The company has rebounded sharply from a troubled period two years ago, when uncertainty over the outlook for Russia's oil industry drove its stock to a low of C$4.70 ($3.38) in late 1995.
Since then, rising revenue in its North American businesses and an improving fiscal and operating climate in Russia has helped lift its stock to its highest level since going public.

Last week, the company reported a 90 percent jump in second-quarter earnings, to C$8 million ($5.7 million), or C19 cents (14 cents) a share, from C$4.5 million ($3.2 million), or C10 cents (7 cents) a share, a year earlier.
Fracmaster fell C75 cents cents) to C$18.50 in midday trading on the Toronto Stock Exchange.
